utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Brdjanin. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. General Talic, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can hear you in a language that I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And you may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours. Good afternoon. My name is Andrew Cayley and I appear on behalf of the Prosecutor with my learned friend Mr. Julian Nicholls together with case manager Denise Gustin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Cayley. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm here with my co-counsel Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Ackerman. Appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic and Ms. Natasha Fauveau for Talic -- General Talic, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Zecevic. Any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour. You will have seen that the solicitors Finers Innocent filed an application for certification for appeal, and I just wanted to inform the Court that the Prosecution is taking a neutral position in respect of that application. Secondly, the next witness based on what the Defence stated yesterday that Ms. Fauveau had some more questions to ask and Mr. Trbojevic indicated he had 15 minutes of cross-examination, will be able at 3.00 to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Cayley. So -- yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: With regard to that request for certificate, we take the same neutral position with regard to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We haven't had time to discuss it as yet. We will be discussing it possibly tomorrow and we will be in a position to hand down our decision by the end of the week. But it's important for us to know that you're putting it on record that you're taking a neutral position. I don't know about the Defence team for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We are -- I'm sorry, Your Honours. But I have to confer with my co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's quite understandable.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Because I'm not aware of what we are talking about at the moment. But we are taking the neutral position as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And you are the least interested in the decision in any case, because ... So later on in the week, please expect a very short decision on certification -- leave for appeal or not. Okay? So witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Zulic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you proceed with your testimony, may I ask you to repeat the solemn declaration once more, please. Hopefully for the last time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir, and you may sit down. Thank you. Madam Fauveau, I just want to make sure that the microphone and headphone, everything is in order. Yes, you may proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you spoke of the day when you were taken to the Partisan cemetery and you said you were taken there by four persons, the same persons that arrested you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So these four persons were three police officers and a driver; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the Partisan cemetery, you saw a group of soldiers wearing olive-grey uniforms; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it not true that the members of the SOS wore the same uniforms?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did, but not their leaders.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You saw another group of persons among whom was Rasula; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And Nemanja Tripkovic was also among that group.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that Nemanja Tripkovic was wearing a camouflage uniform; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask the Prosecutor to show the witness the written statement from 2001, please. It's on page 10 of the English version, third paragraph; and in the Serbo-Croat version, it is page 9, second paragraph from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: In that statement, you said that Nedeljko Rasula and Nemanja Tripkovic were both in civilian clothes. Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have, yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So was Nemanja Tripkovic in civilian clothes or in a uniform?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct that he was in uniform because he never took off that uniform. He was in uniform. That is correct. I know that also because he would come to our village in a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at the sentence prior to that one, you said that Brano Davidovic was the only one in a uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, what he says was "The only one in a military camouflage uniform."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but he said that Tripkovic was in a camouflage uniform as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But with regard to Brano Davidovic, he's not saying that he was the only one in a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you, Mr. President. But it doesn't change my question because according to yesterday's statement, Nemanja Tripkovic was also wearing a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what he is saying today as well. He was saying -- he's repeating that today.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, quite. My question is: Why did he say that Brano Davidovic was the only person in a camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, what's your answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can answer -- I didn't read my diary when I was giving this statement. I gave my diary -- I handed the diary over at the end of my statement and I gave that statement eight years later; therefore, I said straight away that some things I said in the statement, given eight years after the events, naturally I couldn't remember everything. Today it is exactly ten years that I was arrested, on the 18th of June. I didn't want to do this intentionally to -- I repeat that. I will never mention any name intentionally or defame anyone intentionally.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you quite sure that Brano Davidovic was present at the cemetery on that day?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brano Davidovic, how could I not know someone who lives 500 metres away from me? He was my neighbour. And he was chief of police before the war. He was president of the youth organisation in the municipality, the union of socialist youth, as it was called. Who then would I know if not him?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your diary, page 20 of book 1, you enumerated the persons who were present on that day at the Partisan cemetery.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the numbers here. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Why did you not mention Brano Davidovic among those persons?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Probably I didn't remember, because I wrote the diary also after the event, in January 1993, because I need to see -- I was writing this, and as I said I wasn't writing it for anybody except for my children. I didn't mention Brano Davidovic because -- I didn't mention him because I hate him. Unfortunately, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you abide by your statement that Brano Davidovic was at the Partisan cemetery.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Brano Davidovic was still in the police in 1992?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, whether he was in the police or something else, but I think he was some kind of a military commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: An army commander or a commander in the TO, the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether there was any Territorial Defence then. There was no Territorial Defence then. There was the SOS, the 6th Krajina Brigade, Seselj's men, and private military forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you quite sure that Brano Davidovic was not a member of one of those private military forces or of the SOS?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm quite sure he was not in a private army. There was Marko Cevapdzija who led a private army, whom I really don't know. He's from Kruhari.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you quite sure that he was not in the SOS?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke yesterday of a certain Milan Raus. Did you know that person before the war?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That person was a metalworker, I think, by trade. That was his original occupation, and he went to school with me for eight years and he wears a moustache.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war, did he have any military position, any position in the military?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, I don't know what kind of a position he had in the military but I know that he went to the front in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when he returned from the front there?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. But I know that I would see him before the war in various cafes wearing a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that many people wore uniforms in those days in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bosnia? There was the army during the war in Croatia and reserve forces went from Sanski Most to Croatia to the front, and one Muslim, Ramo Nalic -- sorry, two Muslims, Ahmet Hadzic as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question was something else. Is it not true that many persons in Bosnia wore military uniforms at the beginning of 1992?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought you were asking me about 1991. And in 1992 it is true that many people wore uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So many of those people who wore uniforms were not in the army, were they?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do I know who they belonged to? Those I know about I will tell you. What I don't know, I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that there were many people wearing a uniform who did not belong to the regular army in Bosnia at the beginning of 1992?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you spoke of a JNA general, General Daljevic.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you said that that general had retired at the time.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So at the time he was no longer a member of the JNA, was he?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not. In my opinion, he was not in the JNA. But I don't know that; he knows.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you're not sure that General Daljevic was at the Partisan cemetery, are you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that in my statement too. I sat with the man towards the end of 1991 because he has a son-in-law, Slavko Milunovic and he was a colleague of mine working with me and we shared the same office and we were talking. And judging by his face, his appearance, I thought it was he. I can't say a thousand per cent that it was he.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So it is just a supposition on your part.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my supposition. There's another one. That morning a helicopter landed at the stadium in Sanski Most, Podgrmec, opposite the police station. And there's only some 20 metres between them.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday that a certain Simo Simetic was cutting people's throats. This Simo Simetic was in civilian clothes, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: How was he dressed, then?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was wearing some kind of military uniform, a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "a military uniform," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't buttoned up. He had a military shirt on, the type worn by the regular army. He didn't wear a cap.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So it wasn't a complete uniform of the regular army.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He didn't have a cap on his head.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it the same uniform worn by members of the group around him, the same as they wore?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shirt was the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that Rasula ordered Simo Simetic to leave you alone; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you know Rasula's voice well, don't you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you look at your written statement, please, page 10, the one but last paragraph in the English version; and page 10, first paragraph, in the Serbo-Croatian version. You said, didn't you, that it was Mahuna or Macura who told Simo Simetic not to kill you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But after Rasula.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't mention Rasula in your statement.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't? I didn't. I keep telling you it's true that I didn't remember everything eight or nine years later.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your diary, if you look at the page just before the page on which the people present are listed, you just said that you heard a voice which said "That is enough."

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I assume so.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't mention Rasula either in that diary. Why?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't. I didn't write this for the Court. I didn't write down a thousand things. This was written for me, for my own grandchildren.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So this diary contains information that is not correct; is that true?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My diary? My diary?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just didn't write down everything. This is a tenth part of all the things that happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you described the incident when Macura put his pistol in your mouth. And you said that this incident followed the massacre, came after the massacre. However, in your diary - if you look, it is page 17, which is two pages prior to the place where you mentioned the voice that said "That's enough" - you described the same incident but saying that this occurred prior to the massacre.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In book 1?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, book 1. It is two pages prior to the page on which you speak about the person who said "That's enough."

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So what is written in the diary is correct? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I stated is correct. I am saying again that I looked through the diary later on and then I remembered some things that I couldn't think of yesterday, so I didn't answer some questions, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: After what happened at that cemetery -- so the same people took you to the cemetery that took you to Betonirka; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So three policemen and a driver; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke yesterday of your transfer to Manjaca, and you said that the people who put you on that truck were policemen. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And these policemen accompanied you to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And these policemen --

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, I don't know whether they escorted us or someone else. I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And when you arrived at Manjaca, did you see those policemen there or did you not see them?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw them there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And during the trip, you had a bottle of aftershave lotion with you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: How were you able to keep that bottle at Betonirka?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tonci brought it for me, the man I spoke about, saying that he was the person who opened the door, who would bring us food. And I looked for him after the war, but unfortunately he's no longer among the living because he assisted Muslims. Both he and his shift of five men, they gave us food and water, as much as they had. And they never took people out when they were on duty at night to beat them. They didn't take them out to christen them or anything. So I feel duty-bound towards them because they probably saved my life. And it is my duty to show them every respect, even though they are Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Once you entered Manjaca, you did receive water, didn't you? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From whom? From those detainees of ours who arrived with us in the convoy? And it was only once we entered the garage that they brought us water. But that was one cup of two decilitres of water per person. I said that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you were given water once you entered the garages at Manjaca; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. But I must repeat again: For a person who had been -- who has been travelling - I don't know exactly for how long - but roughly from 11.00 until the sun started setting. Would one decilitre of water be sufficient? If you think that's sufficient, then there's nothing I can say.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you mentioned 2 decilitres. Was it 1 or 2?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please don't confuse me. I didn't say 2 decilitres. 2 decilitres were shared by two men.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's not what you said, but I shall move on to another question. After entering Manjaca you were examined by a doctor, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the third day I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And later a doctor of the Red Cross examined you as well.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the doctor from Manjaca examine you later again as well?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't examine me later on. He hid some medicines and he said to me that they would kill me -- kill him for these couple of small bottles that he brought me to drink if they knew he had given them to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday that you ate grass at Manjaca. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us when you ate grass.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I ate grass as soon as I started walking around a bit and was able to pick some grass, I ate grass until aid arrived from the Red Cross. It wasn't just me that ate grass; others did too.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please specify the date approximately of the day when you ate grass and were beaten after that.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say that anywhere. I can't.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: In any event, it was after the arrival of the Red Cross at the camp; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the arrival of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even before I would graze a little, and it was best around the toilet. It was highest.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: The occasion I'm referring to, when you were beaten after that, was that after the Red Cross arrived at Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you continued eating grass even though the Red Cross brought food.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. The Red Cross didn't bring food until sometime around the 28th or the 30th of August. I don't know exactly, but I think it was the 28th or the 30th of August. And the first time the Red Cross -- I'm saying from memory now -- the date when Mr. Michel [phoen] - I can't look it up in the diary now - came. Now, whether that was the 17th or the 20th of July when he came for the first time and that was the first time that we were brought some cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So between the 17th of July and the 30th of August, the Red Cross did not bring any food?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you write down in your diary that you ate grass at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did, but I don't know. But I think I did. I wrote down that he slapped me because I was eating grass. Not just me; Ahmet Alisic, Osman Hodzic, all of those who left the line to pick grass were hit like this on the head. But later on - I have to point this out - when Spaga came, he brought Alisic Ahmet some food so that he couldn't eat grass. But that young man had terrible diarrhoea.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about the death of Omer Filipovic. Did you see Omer Filipovic being killed?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see Omer Filipovic's body?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And Esad Bender's.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you see Omer Filipovic's body?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it when they were carrying it in the morning, at 6.00 in the morning from the stables. They called the -- what they called the clinic. It was a horse stable. It's a small building which is covered, and that's where the bodies were.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And where were you at 6.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were going to breakfast. And we had been lined up facing downwards because at Manjaca where the stables are, it's a slope. You look from -- you look downwards, and you can see everything right up to the road down there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that the prisoners had to clean the camp before international persons visited it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you said that the prisoners who had more clothes had to arrange their clothes, they had to sort them. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So some prisoners had clothes that they could use to change into; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if they even had a coat and a shirt, they would wear that coat in the middle of summer. They would hang it up in the afternoon somewhere because there was only a roof up there and it was terrible. It was so hot. There was no attic. So the heat was just unbearable inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about Muhamed Boskovic, and you said that he was in charge of facilitating relations between prisoners and the camp command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And Muhamed Boskovic was also a prisoner, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And in fact, he was your representative with the camp command; is that correct -- at the camp command?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he was, but he communicated with the command. He was in contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And he protected the prisoners' interests.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. But he was always beaten for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: After you had arrived at the camp from the 17th of July, the Red Cross visited the camp on a regular basis; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every 15 days.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true to say that certain prisoner groups were released after you -- before you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One group, whose legs had been broken and their arms, they were released and they went off to England. Mr. Bernard Kouchner promised them that he would get them out of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But other prisoners had been released before the release of this group; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct. That's true. They were people who were underage, who weren't adults, and people over 60 years of age.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your diary - it's the third book -- it's in the third book of your diary - you said that you were more sure -- that you were in greater safety in the camps than your family which was at liberty; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, could you please direct the witness straight to the part of his diary to which you are referring.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the third book, page 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 15 in the original or --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the original, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So in the English translation, it would be page what?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the translation isn't necessary. I'll answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But we need to know exactly what you said in the diary. At least how does the paragraph start, the words in the beginning of the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's true that I wrote that I was in greater safety at Manjaca than my family was. I wrote that. But that was when a woman came who was always -- a woman from the International Red Cross. She was present at all times and supervised the recovery of the prisoners. She was there every day, so those -- no one was maltreated then. It was no longer as it was up until the 30th of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: In fact you said that twice. You said on two occasions - in August for the first time and in the month of October for the second time - is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say "from August," from August things were easier. I haven't found that. But if in the diary it says from September or October -- but from August onwards I said that that's when discipline became a little more lax. There were no longer beatings, maltreatment, because -- as Bula was replaced -- Kovacevic came and replaced him. Kovacevic, also known as Spaga. That's when discipline was no longer so terrible. When Kovacevic came, I no longer saw Bula.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, Madam Fauveau, may I refer you to the book 3, English version, page 6, bottom of the page, last five lines. "That Thursday I was slapped by a Chetnik because I had picked a dandelion to eat it, hungry as I was. Many people ate grass. I just wasn't lucky, so I got slapped. He cursed my mother on account of my grazing on Serbian grass. They would do this to anyone they caught eating grass or walking on it." That's because earlier on you --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. President. But in the Serbo-Croat version, which I have used, the copy is pretty bad. It's certainly a part that I was not able to read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that you had been liberated from Manjaca on the 23rd of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The 22nd or the 24th, but I was released towards the end of November.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it true to say that you were released on the 14th of November, 1992?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you allow for the possibility that it was on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been better if I'd been released on the 18th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And when you were released, there were still prisoners in the camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And in fact this camp was closed one month later; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the hearing of the 7th of June, 1992 you said that you had been released together with Judge Draganovic. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Wasn't Judge Draganovic in fact released one month later than you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know I was with him in Karlovac and in Cologne. We went to Cologne together.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And up until what date were you in Karlovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until just before Christmas, a day before Christmas we arrived in Cologne.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you would allow for the possibility that Judge Draganovic joined you in Karlovac in the middle of December.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's possible. It's possible he was released then. I know that all those over 45 years of age were released -- were released from Manjaca, and that someone underage was -- remained in Manjaca and they wouldn't let him go.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in The Hague, you provided the Prosecutor with a notebook that you had in Manjaca. How did you receive this notebook?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was sent a packet from -- to Manjaca from Banja Luka and clothes and food and cigarettes. A Serb did this. No one touched this parcel; I have to say that. It wasn't opened. No one opened it. Because whoever got a carton of cigarettes in Manjaca, that person was a real capitalist.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: When did you receive this notebook?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In August. I received the parcel in August.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And in fact in this notebook there were certain notes, there were certain telephone numbers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct. Because on the message that I received -- in the message I received, they thought we would be leaving -- we would be released on the 30th of August via the intermediary of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said on the 7th of June that you had written your diary, the one that you wrote later on, so that no one would ever forget what had happened; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not so that no one would forget. You have misunderstood it. Read the title -- or maybe someone translated it incorrectly.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: In any event, that's what it says in the transcript on page 6849 of the version -- of the French version. I'm referring to the title "So that your grandchildren will never forget what happened"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you also said that you hadn't written down everything in this diary so as not to affect the people, contaminate the people for whom this had been written; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you yourself selected events that would best be forgotten; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Because there was a war in the Balkans every 40 to 50 years. And if I incited hatred among my grandchildren, then they again would have to live through war, through expulsions. Either they would have to do so or Serbs or Croats. Because I want my grandchildren to live in peace, since I wasn't able to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: On page 2 of this diary you wrote a sentence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first one. It's right at the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you said "The Serbs as the Serbs are doing their work and are preparing for massacres."

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you want to say that the Serbs -- what was characteristic of the Serbs was that they would prepare for massacres?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but that they would sit down and eat with you and then they would be capable of killing you, because all of these people that I know I've eaten with them all, went to their houses, I've had drinks with them, installed central heating in their houses, sorted out the water. Some went to schools with some of them. Some of them were my teachers. Others were my children's teachers. Some of them were even personal friends who surprised me. But there were some who didn't surprise me. Some were incredibly terrible. And I thank them for now.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: This sentence in fact, it's one of your opinions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I expressed my opinion. They told us when we had a joint meeting of all the local communes, Podbrijezje, Sanski Most, they said we'd hold hands, we'll go to the municipality so that they don't make us quarrel among ourselves. And a few days later they said, "You go on your own patrols. We won't go with you."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the end of your diary - it's the very last sentence in book 3, the last sentence in your diary - you said something from Jajce -- of a man from Jajce. You said that this man from Jajce said that the Croats were worse than the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it true that you personally didn't have any experiences with the Croats?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I had experiences with Croats. They're friends of mine, like the Serbs. I still have today. But that prisoner from Jajce, what he said, that was his opinion. I just wrote it down.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But nevertheless you thought that your grandchildren should know that the Croats were bad too.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You didn't mention that I mentioned Muslims in my diary too, that they took food and smuggled it. It's all the same to me. If someone is dishonest, he's dishonest.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the hearing of the 7th of June, you said that you had written this diary in December 1992 and January 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you have a look at your statement of 2001. It's page 15 in the English version and it's the third paragraph, which is in fact a sentence. And it's page 14, the second paragraph, which is also a sentence, in the Serbo-Croat version. In the preceding paragraph, you spoke about the 20th of August, 1992. And then you said: [In English] "I made no diary entries after this date." [Interpretation] Did you write a diary in Manjaca itself?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I wrote a diary in Manjaca from August, this one, this small one, and not this bundle here.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But in this notebook there is no date.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which notebook?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the notebook that you used in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean there's no date? There are dates. Not all of the dates, but certain dates are there. And what I could remember, I wrote that down. 28th of August, 29th of August, the 30th of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: On what page is that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's on the third page here, the third sheet, so that would be the sixth page then. But I didn't use this when I was writing this diary. So maybe I changed the dates. Maybe I mixed up the dates in the diary, moved them. Because when I was writing this, I didn't have these things. I went from Cologne and only saw my wife and children for a few hours and I left the notebook with her so that she could phone Germany so that she could know whom to call for help, because I didn't know where I was going to in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know which copy the witness has, but there are no dates in the copy that I have. That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I apologise. Mr. Zulic, you've heard what Madam Fauveau has just pointed out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you start with this particular diary, the one you kept in Manjaca. Do you have it in front of you? Yes. Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And going -- starting from the first page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this has been torn up, this cover part, and I'm very ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you show us at least one page on which there is a date. That will make the life of everyone easier. On the ELMO, yes. We could put it on the ELMO, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The events that appear on this page, these are events that would have nothing to do with your detention in Manjaca; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but these are events which are related -- this is related with the event that took place in Sana -- in Sanski Most, Mahala.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For example, I see in what seems to be the penultimate page -- not exactly the penultimate but -- there is on the left-hand side of the page written vertically in the margin "26 May," then there is another word which I can't read. Perhaps the witness can enlighten us on it. I don't know if it's important. Because if it's not important, let's move to the next -- to the next question, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going back to the diary that you wrote in December 1992 and January 1993. On page 1 of your diary at the very beginning you speak of Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: We're you in Bijeljina in 1992?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't, but I watched television. I had a TV set.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Which television station were you able to watch?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sarajevo Television in those days.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So until May 1992 you were able to watch Sarajevo Television; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you personally did not see what was happening in Bijeljina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not, but I saw on television when Madam Biljana Plavsic was kissing Arkan, and I saw Fikret Abdic on television.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned Selo Ravno. You personally didn't see what happened there, did you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't, but I saw everything on television perfectly.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And as for Mostar, you weren't there either.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. This was just a chronology of events, what happened before Sanski Most. I saw Alija Izetbegovic on a tank telling the people that there would be no war. And then the Croats - I can't remember their names - down there in Herzegovina, that was on television too.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also speak of Foca. You were not in Foca either, were you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was also on the basis of television reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: On page 3 you speak of Bosanski Novi, Prijedor, and Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you in Bosanski Novi in 1992?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But refugees came from Bosanski Novi -- Ahmet and Dina. I don't remember the surname. He's Mehemed Drobic's brother-in-law, my next-door neighbour. He spoke about it and said that the place had been occupied, that refugees had been rounded up, put on a train, and transported abroad. That is what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it not true that in your diary you describe many events of which you have no personal knowledge?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Surely images on the TV screen are sufficient that one sees. If something is shown on television -- for instance, you would say that Alija Izetbegovic was not on a JNA tank saying that there would be no war, but this was featured in public on television. Also on television we saw Biljana Plavsic kissing Arkan; then also that Fikret Abdic was captured. I remember very well that he was lying on the ground in Bijeljina. This was on television. This was not montage. If you think, madam, that some things cannot be verified, you are wrong. They can easily.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also speak of events in Prijedor. Regarding the events in Prijedor and Bosanski Novi, you didn't see them on television.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But I learnt from the refugees what was going on. They came through the woods.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you personally have no means of verifying whether the version told you by these persons was indeed the truth.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why did I have to verify when you could hear the shells from Prijedor, in Kozarac too you can hear the cannonade from heavy guns. Not rifle fire but guns and tanks and heavy artillery. I assume that is what they were -- can be heard. So you go out during the night at 1.00 a.m. and you can hear it. Also refugees were coming from Prijedor and Kozarac through the woods, and they were saying and telling what was going on. I didn't write down that I was in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: In any event, you have no possibility of checking what exactly happened in Prijedor, Kozarac, or Bosanski Novi; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, objection. It's been asked and it's been answered about three times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Objection sustained. Next question, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you speak of rape, murder in Prijedor, how could you know that there were any such instances?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, through the refugees, from the refugees. Unfortunately after the war it proved to be true. I didn't know it at the time, but the refugees who came through the woods spoke about it. And when the war ended, it was the truth. I didn't claim that these things happened. I noted down what the refugees said as they arrived. In Podbrijezje was a place for refugees. That is why it wasn't immediately shelled straight away.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: What you wrote in your diary is in Prijedor a war is being raged -- or rather, cleansing, burning down of the city, murders of Muslims, rapes.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Ljubinka Hilmije came from Prijedor with her two sons. Her husband had been killed in his house, in the apartment and she came to stay with Fadil Jakupovic, her brother-in-law, and that is what she said. I didn't make it up. Jakupovic was killed in his own apartment.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: In any event you personally did not see any murder.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. But I wrote down what they told me. And unfortunately when I returned home in 1996, it is true that Hilmije Jakupovic was killed in 1992. So the woman told the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But is it also true that at the time when you wrote that down you didn't know that that was the truth?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... next question, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it not true that this diary is more of impressions on your part than a recounting of the truth?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what your understanding is, but you have now given me the strength to write down everything that happened. I never thought of completing this, but now you have given me the impetus. You haven't angered me at all. You have given me the will to really finish something that I never intended to finish. Thank you for doing that for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Aren't you afraid that your grandchildren will have a distorted impression of events?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They will not have a distorted version. They will only then know the real truth. Only then will they get the whole truth, because I'll go around and collect information about events and write things down. You've just encouraged me to do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Aren't you afraid of conveying to them a feeling of hatred towards other nations?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau. Mr. Trbojevic, you have a cross-examination to do. I think we will have to leave it for -- until after 4.00, because we're going to have a break now, rather than starting and stopping you after the first question we'll break and you will commence your cross-examination immediately after the break. In the meantime, Mr. Cayley, please have the other -- the next witness ready, because I would anticipate that this cross-examination not to last long. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll have a break now. We will resume at 4.00. Thank you. -- Recess taken at 3.44 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, everyone, for the delay. But it was unavoidable unfortunately. Yes. Mr. Trbojevic -- Mr. Zulic, there's going to be now a -- another cross-examination from the co-counsel appearing for Radoslav Brdjanin. Mr. Trbojevic, the witness is in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zulic, on page 6 of your statement to the Prosecution, you explained --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which statement, please? Of 2001 or of 2000?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 6 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 14th of June, 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Serbian version, fourth paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Have you found it, please?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 27th of May? Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There is your description that the population of Mahala were gathered at the soccer field in Krkojevci, whereas the population of Muhici at the driving school training ground. You said that you heard this on the radio.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were invited over the radio to leave their houses to -- so that the Serb forces could deal with the Green Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: So your conclusion was that this announcement on Radio Sana was correct.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I thought; it was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: But yesterday you also said that an announcement on the same radio when reporting about the attack of the Green Berets at Hrustovo was not correct.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not Hrustovo but Cirkici as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: You also said yesterday that there was a report on the same radio station about an attack on Vrhpolje mentioning the casualties on the Serb side, dead and wounded.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I didn't say that yesterday. Vrhpolje? I don't think there was any mention of Vrhpolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: But did you know that that was not true?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that this was announced on Radio Sanski Most, but I learnt from the refugees when they arrived in Podbrijezje what was going on. That is true. When the refugees came, when they were brought to Podbrijezje from the school, then I learnt that that was unfortunately true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately it is quite clear to me that there's no logic which would help us to establish what the witness thought listening to the radio, what when he was listening to the refugees, what when he made notes in one diary and what when we made notes in another diary and what he's saying today, so that I can just draw attention to these differences and discrepancies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's a submission. You will have ample time to make it in due course, and you will definitely not be stopped. But you are going to be stopped now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm sorry. I've finished with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: On page 7 of that same statement, second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Second paragraph in the Serbo-Croat version or in the English version? I suppose --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Second full paragraph, [B/C/S spoken]. Is that the one?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The year is 1996. "In 1996."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So for the record -- for the record we're referring to page 7 in the English version, the third paragraph before the -- before the end, starting "In 1996."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have found it. "In 1996 --"

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the Bosnian army did not wish you to film Mahala so you did it secretly and that Mahala looked approximately like it did in 1992.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Will you tell us, do you know why they didn't want you to film it?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know. I was with foreign license plates, German license plates, and I didn't have permission to film. No one knew who was doing the filming in 1996 and for what purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain to us in what respect was it approximately the same?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation was approximately the same. That means that the houses through donations of international organisations for roofs, windows, doors, roof tiles were given.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: So you meant that repairs had started.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, try to allow a pause between the statement of the witness and your next question, because if you jump straight in you will create difficulties for the interpreters. And the same applies to you, sir. Try to allow -- allow an interval of time before you start answering. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: On page 8 of the same statement -- it's the one but last paragraph in the Serbian version. Have you found it, Mr. Zulic?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: You described the situation in the garage. And you said among other things that the guards would not allow you to go to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Only after Tonci and his shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: But is it true that you did leave the garage for meals?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did go out and we had to eat; otherwise he would cock his pistol and say, "Who doesn't finish in two minutes, I'll shoot at his head." And --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: You've told us that. I'm just trying to establish whether it was possible to leave the garage several times a day.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is correct that that was possible for two minutes. That was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's fine. Let's move on. On page 9 of this statement, the paragraph beginning with the words "Around the 22nd of June."

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: "On about the 22nd of June, 1992." It says that you went down towards the stream through the bushes and then you were given a hoe and told to dig your own grave. "There were already 20 to 25 men doing the same thing when I arrived there," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday in your testimony you said that they gave you a hoe but you didn't say that they told you what to do.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember saying that they didn't tell me what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: So did they tell you or didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's clarify this, because it could well be a matter -- a question of interpretation. But as far as I can remember - and usually my memory doesn't fail me that much - the question that was put to the witness yesterday was not whether he was told what to do but whether he was told what he was going to dig for, what was the purpose for the digging. And he replied yesterday that he was not told what he was going to dig for but he arrived at a conclusion. I mean, it's being interpreted now -- what your question was: "Yesterday in your testimony you said that they gave you a hoe but you didn't say what they told you -- that they told you what to do." It may well be a question of interpretation. I don't know, because I can't follow from the B/C/S into English. But what's your comment, Mr. Zulic, if there is a comment to make? Do you have a question, basically, because you --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I explained my question. In the statement it says that he was told to dig his own grave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is: Did they say that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did. But yesterday nobody asked me whether they told me that. His Honour, the Judge is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Move to the next question, Mr. Trbojevic, because it's -- because I can't be right and wrong at the same time. So move to the next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: In your description of that undoubtedly horrific event was not completed. Did this group of people actually dig 20 or so graves or not?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They couldn't dig them; just as I couldn't. They could have dug 30 or 50 -- a hole 30 or 50 centimetres deep because of the soil.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He explained that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Let's go on to page 11, then, in which you refer to your arrival at Manjaca. Page 11 in the Serbian language, third paragraph. Have you found it, Mr. Zulic?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that -- please ask me your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of that paragraph, you say that men armed with rifles were on guard and that they were wearing Chetnik garb. What kind of garb was it?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: How did Chetnik garb differ from other camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no difference. They're all Chetniks to me. For me, if they kept me in a camp, they were Chetniks. I didn't make up their name. Draza Mihajlovic [phoen] gave them that name. If I was named Ahmet they shouldn't be insulted by this, because they also were prone to sing Chetnik songs. So why couldn't I call them that? I didn't name them like that. I'm not to blame that somebody gave me Ahmet as a name, that someone -- my parents named me Ahmet. It was my parents' fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you've answered in greater detail than I had expected -- or rather, more sincerely that I had expected. Talking about this trip to Manjaca, you told us that you set off around 11.00.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: And that the journey lasted until the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the sunset, something like that. I didn't have a watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: My question is: How is it possible that you were so thirsty with all due respect for the inhuman conditions and the heat and the high temperature and everything for you to decide to drink your shaving lotion? You're a serious person. You know that most of the content in a shaving lotion is alcohol.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll give you an answer. But on that day the temperature was extremely high. Let me ask you what you would have done to survive. When you simply see people dropping just like that. 64 men covered by canvas. Allow me to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him finish, please, Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very good at maths, but I know from medicine that a person needs 3 cubic metres of air per minute [Realtime transcript read in error "American"]. And 64 men in a truck 5 by 2 and a half with a tarpaulin about 3 metres high, work out the volume and you will see how much air there was and how much water the people needed. The arithmetic is very simple. Take a pen, multiply width by length and height, you will get the volume and you will be able to calculate how much air there was inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just trying to draw attention to the fact that you don't put out a fire with petrol nor do you quench your thirst with alcohol?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just thinking of how I could quench my thirst. I thought about it. I saw people dying, so I thought that I might die. And if I hadn't done that, I may not be sitting here today with you. Maybe you'd prefer it if I wasn't here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. Why?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Could I ask you to tell us how you did that operation -- carried out that operation, the taking of urine and its use.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Very simply. When I drank the aftershave lotion, I took -- I urinated. I didn't know that I was passing blood at the time. I didn't see that. I removed the boy's head from my lap. And then this took place -- and then peed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, line 11 says that three cubic metres of air per American. I think -- I think that must be something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Three cubic metres of air per person. That's what -- that's what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whether or not that is correct or not, I don't know, because I'm not familiar with how much air.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Us Americans do need quite a bit of air.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They carry it with them sometimes as well, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's right. We get pretty hot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Trbojevic, please let's get it over and done with. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I have to ask the witness whether he stands by his claim that a loaf of bread of 800 grammes was divided into 44 parts.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. A loaf of 800 grammes, 22 slices would be cut, and then you would cut those slices along the length. And then it depended who would get a gramme extra or more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that that would work out to 18 grammes per slice?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: It's impossible to cut such slices with a knife.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. Give me a soldier's loaf of bread and I'll cut it up and you'll see that it's possible and give me a knife. I'll show you how this is done. That's why I ate grass.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Trbojevic. Is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, your testimony, your evidence here has finally come to an end. I wish to thank you for having come over to give evidence and you will now be escorted by the usher and taken care of and returned to where you want to go. I thank you once more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Thank you, Your Honours. And I would like to thank the Prosecution too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is the next witness ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The next witness is ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought so. So Mr. Nicholls will be handling the next witness. What we don't have is an indication of what documents we will be -- you will be using. And incidentally, before I forget, with regard to the previous witness there is the sketch he drew of Manjaca camp, which was indicated to us as being possibly -- being made use of by Defence for -- you're not making use of it. Because it was also given a -- an exhibit number, DB80-something, I think or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I firmly believed it was going to be used, Your Honour, but it was not, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: DB89.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I suspect what we'll do is withdraw it as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Madam Registrar, do you have it on record as it being exhibit DB89, or not yet?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Not yet. It's never been used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I take it that it is not being tendered. So remove that, DB89.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, on the issue of exhibits, my understanding is the exhibits for this witness were tendered and admitted, which is why I haven't mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All of them. There are no exhibits forthcoming from the Defence but all the exhibits tendered by the Prosecution have been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You can admit -- bring forward the witness, please. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are no protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And with this witness, Your Honour, there will be some exhibits. I'm sorry, we -- I thought a list had been provided. But we have them and will pass them out as we come to them. There will be very, very few.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Mr. Faik Biscevic, good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before addressing you any further, I think it is my duty to apologise to you for having kept you here waiting from 3.00. This was not done capriciously, but it was something that we had to do because the testimony of the previous witness took longer than we had anticipated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for your understanding. Now, you will -- may I ask you to stand up, please. The usher standing next to you is going to give you the text of a solemn declaration that you are required to make here in open court before you start giving evidence. It is a declaration to tell us the truth. It's the equivalent of an oath, in other words. Can I ask you to proceed with making that declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we start giving evidence -- you start giving evidence, may I explain to you a little bit where you are and who you are surrounded with. You see here us three. I'm the Presiding Judge and I am flanked by two other Judges, that together we form this Trial Chamber -- we compose this Trial Chamber. I am -- my name is Agius and I come from Malta. To my right is Judge Janu from the Czech Republic ask to my left is Judge Taya from Japan. The persons right in front of us is the Registry personnel. And then to your right in the front row you have -- you see three persons. That's the team for the Prosecution that is handling this case. And the gentleman at the -- furthest -- at the extreme left -- extreme right is the -- is counsel who will be conducting the examination-in-chief. And to your left in the front row there are two teams for the Defence. The first team is the Defence team for accused Brdjanin, Radoslav Brdjanin, and the last two persons are the Defence team for General Talic. I think with that we can proceed. The procedure is that you will first be asked a series of questions by the Prosecution, at the end of which - and that could be today or it could be tomorrow, I don't know - you will then be cross-examined separately by the two Defence teams. After that, you may have some questions directed to you from the Bench, from the Judges themselves, and also possibly a re-examination. Mr. Nicholls, you may proceed with the examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Biscevic, I'd like to start with briefly going through your background. You were born in June 1940 in Prijedor municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then nearly right away, before you were one years old, your family and you moved to Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
