utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: For the next 52 years, until 1992, you lived almost exclusively in Sanski Most, other than a few years away for schooling and in your military service.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And in Sanski Most before 1992, you worked as a dentist, and I believe you had actually two practices.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Another business which you had was a goldsmith shop which was in Sanski Most town which sold jewellery and also you would repair jewellery in that shop.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You were married, and in 1992 you lived with your wife and your three sons.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And one of your sons worked with you in your dental practice and the other two at that point were training to be dentists so that they could join you later.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, in November 1992 you left -- you were transferred from Manjaca camp at that point to Croatia and you returned permanently to Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, in 1995.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that's where you live now and you are still a practicing dentist there with one of your sons.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I want to go back to 1989 and talk about your political activities and some meetings which you attended. Now, prior -- before 1989 were you active in politics or interested in politics?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But then you became the first President of the SDA party in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could you just tell the Chamber when you became president and how long you served as President of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: After the annual assembly in Sanski Most in 1990, I became the President of the SDA party in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how long were you president for?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: For one year, one term of office. One year later there were re-elections and I wasn't a candidate at those elections. Someone else came. Someone else was appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, even after you stopped serving as president, did you remain active in SDA politics as a member of the main board?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And during that time, around -- throughout 1990, could you tell me -- tell us what relationships were like between Serbs and non-Serbs in Sanski Most, and also between the three political parties.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: At that time the relations between the Serbs and non-Serbs were quite normal. First of all, the Party of Democratic Action was formed and both Serbs and Catholics were in it. Mr. Rasula Nedeljko and Mr. Ante Tunic were among them. And at the end of the assembly session they congratulated me and they went to celebrate with me because they had been invited.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You mentioned Mr. Rasula. That's Nedeljko Rasula. Could you please explain to me who that person was and how you know him. When did you first meet him, for instance?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Nedeljko Rasula was the President of the SDS of the other party in Sanski Most. But before that Mr. Nedeljko Rasula was a teacher. We both went to the same secondary school, so we knew each other personally. He was a patient of mine. He would come to my practice for dental treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, after you stopped acting as president and -- but continued to remain active with the SDA as a board member, did you attend meetings, municipality meetings and SDA meetings?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mostly all the meetings, unless I was prevented from doing so or unless I was travelling somewhere. I would always attend, and I would decide on all the issues on the agenda, on all the problems that would arise at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, these meetings you've talked about, did Mr. Rasula also attend these meetings?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: In general, if it was the municipal assembly or if there was some sort of inter-party agreement, then Rasula would be present. He was the first president and then he was the mayor and he was replaced by Vlado Vrkes who was the president of the party. So Mr. Rasula in general attended all the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Moving up to 1991 and 1992 specifically, how many meetings of any kind do you believe you attended where Mr. Rasula was also present?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, at least a hundred which we attended, in the course of 1991 and 1992. Approximately that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, at these meetings, to the best of your memory - because it was ten years ago - would Mr. Rasula take notes during the meetings?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rasula was a professor. He was a very orderly man. He had a nice characteristic. And regardless of who was leading a meeting, whether it was he himself or someone else, he would keep his own private notes. He would take his own notes and he would make a summary at the end. He would make a note of the date, and he would put down his signature, he would sign it. That was something specific to him. And next to his name he would put the name -- his father's name and his surname. We often laughed about this but his father died in the course of the Second World War and as a sign of gratitude he would put down his father's name next to his signature. That was something that was characteristic of him. Not everyone would do this, and this is -- in this way, he was different from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. My question was specifically: Did he take notes? And you've answered that he did. Is this something which you personally observed?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You need to answer verbally, because we're recording this hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It's important that you say either "yes" or "no." Because otherwise, if you nod it won't go into the records. Thank you. So your answer was or is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said yes, as we formed three parties we were in all respects the political authorities in Sanski Most. We were those who were in power. And now it was necessary to establish some sort of authority, solve those problems. The meetings when they were held, if I was presiding I would be in the middle and the President of the HDZ, Mr. Tunic, or the SDS President, Mr. Rasula would be by my sides or it would be the other way around. If it was Rasula who was presiding or Ante, we would be sitting next to them. At the beginning we were in general, together and later, if there were inter-party agreements for example between the SDA and the SDS then the representatives of the SDS, the main board, they would sit on one side of the table and we would sit on the other side of the table. And the two of us we sat opposite each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Try to answer the question, the whole question, and nothing but the question, leaving other matters for the time being until you are asked about other matters. The question was whether you can confirm by simply saying yes or no that from your personal experience you know that Mr. Rasula kept notes. This is something that you personally observed. That was the question. Please answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Nicholls, your next question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's right, as I discussed with you, if you can try to answer the question that I ask you, we'll move on more quickly and we'll cover everything more -- more efficiently. While you observed Mr. Rasula making notes at these meetings when you were either sitting next to him or across from him in the room, do you remember what kind of -- what method he would use? Whether he used loose-leaf paper, whether he wrote in a book or a binder, if you can describe what he took notes on.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: In Bosnia and Herzegovina it was the custom for companies or enterprises to give as gifts to friends or businessmen who held some sort of posts, they would give them special diaries which were valid for about a year. They had a certain size and they had -- they included a calendar, the days for the entire year, so it was possible to make notes for a certain day in such diaries. And if such a diary was given as a present, you'd have the name of the company up at the top so that you would know which company had given this as a present. But it was possible to buy such diaries in book shops and in such a case you wouldn't have a heading. That was the difference. They were either red or -- they were either black or a sort of dark yellow colour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Rasula's, what kind of diary or whatever did he use that you know of, that you can tell us, to take his notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a diary. It was a diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was a diary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you describe it? I'm trying to take over a little bit because otherwise we'll never get there. Can you describe it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if I could add specifically for 1992. Can you remember what sort of diary he used to keep notes in?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Not only he had it. These were standard diaries, 25 by 15. That was the size. Not only Rasula had it, but I had such a diary and other people had such diaries too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Biscevic, more or less between October and mid-January, if not February, in my country I get something like 20, 30, 40 different diaries which I never use. But if I use one of them and I want to explain to you which one I'm using, I have to describe it. This is what is being asked from you. Can you remember -- can you describe this diary that you saw Mr. Rasula take -- put down notes in? Can you describe it? Did it have a cover? Did the cover have a colour? This is what we want to know, not the size or whether it was a diary or not. We have understood that it was a diary. But can you describe it? In other words, if we were to go looking for a diary possibly kept by Mr. Rasula, what should we -- what should we be looking for? How are we going to identify this diary from so many others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the diaries were either black or dark coffee colour. I don't know why this diary is important. I didn't pay attention to it. But I'm telling you in general what the diaries look like and what sort Rasula had, what he used to make notes and what I made -- used to make notes. It was black, as I said. He was orderly, and he kept this diary in an orderly way, in a more orderly way than we did. That was what was specific about him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. What I'd like to do now is show an item to the witness and see if he can recognise it. This is not something that we're planning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. Before you do that, perhaps you can ask him whether there is anything else that he can recall that could help us identify the diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You've heard the question, sir. If you could answer His Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you ever observe him writing in this diary near enough to see how he wrote?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we sat next to each other. Yes, I was very near him, at most of the meetings. As we were presidents. So we would sit next to each other, on the whole. And these diaries -- I'll repeat this again -- they are standard diaries. You can have a hundred such diaries which are all identical. It wasn't only Rasula who had such a diary or only myself. Hundreds of such diaries were issued and used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not going to put any direct questions myself, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could show this object to the witness. It's -- I'll identify it by its ERN number for the record. It's 01363236 through 01363305. And Ms. Gustin has that item.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, if it can -- if it can be taken out of that plastic -- I don't know whether it can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. I'd prefer we don't do that. That's a chain of custody item.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I wondered, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So I'd also like to state for the record that the witness is having to look at that item through a plastic covering and envelope which he's not able to open.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And your question is?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: My question is: If you can remember, does that look like or is that one of the diaries you've been describing to us? You've told us that there were many. Is that similar to or not similar to the diary which you saw Mr. Rasula recording notes in at meetings in 1992? And you can pick it up or hold it. Just don't open the envelope.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Diaries of this kind were those that we had. Now, whether this is Rasula's or not is not something I can claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. But --

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: But this type of diary we did have in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you can tell me -- my question is not whether that is Mr. Rasula's diary but whether that is -- as you've said, is of the type you had. Is that of the type which he used?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That is the type, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, moving on, you've told us that in the beginning when you were President of the SDA the relationships with the other parties and between Serbs and non-Serbs in general in Sanski Most were -- were good or correct, were normal. When did these good or normal relationships start to break down?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: There was a war in Slovenia that lasted some ten days or so and it was over. Then the war moved to Croatia. When the war started in Croatia, there was a mass call-up into the reserve forces of the Yugoslav People's Army among Muslims and Croats who were rounded up and sent to the front in Croatia. At that very moment we were faced with a dilemma as to what should be done. Since the war was already on in Croatia, there were large numbers of fighters, reservists coming back and when they would get to Sanski Most they would get drunk, start shooting, throw hand grenades, and provoke the Muslims and Croats. And that is when in certain businesses started to be destroyed over the night. During the night we would hear that it had happened the next day. Though we didn't know what was really going on or who was behind it. In the meantime, as we saw that the war was ongoing in Croatia, our relationships started to break down from that moment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was the SDA position on the mobilisation and whether Bosniak men from Sanski Most should go and fight in that war?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: The position of the Yugoslav People's Army was that you were drafted and you have to go where you are sent, where it is necessary. And the need for that existed in the Republic of Croatia, which was in those days a Yugoslav republic, a republic of Yugoslavia. However, as our businesses were being blown up, we said that if our boys are going to be called up, they should not go to Croatia, they should remain in Bosnia and Herzegovina. If they are sent to Croatia, then we would not let the Muslims and Croats go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you talked about these problems with soldiers returning from Croatia, blowing up property, and drinking. Were these incidents investigated by the police, these crimes?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The police did investigate those crimes, but they never discovered anything. Then we requested that we should have mixed patrols during the night consisting of Serbs, Croats, and Muslims who would put on uniforms so that people would know that they're officials to try and establish who was -- who were the perpetrators. However, the military department -- the head of the military department specifically, said that they were doing their work properly and when they discovered what would happen, they would let us know. But nothing came of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did these incidents of bombings and shootings at night, did that continue on after, or was it ever stopped by the military police?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: It continued on a nightly basis. Then they started getting drunk during the daytime too, because Serb soldiers coming from the front could freely carry weapons. There were no restrictions. And the army protected them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to --

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: They could do what they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just to be clear, could you tell me what time period you're talking about now when you're describing these incidents of soldiers causing problems.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: This was the period of roughly the spring of 1992. End of 1991 and the spring of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And were these problems which you've talked about, were those discussed at municipality meetings at which you were present, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: All meetings that were being held at the time - and they were held almost every day, both in the municipality and in the military department attached to the Secretariat for Defence and in the MUP - I attended too, being a member of the main board.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But at these meetings you weren't able to resolve these problems and stop these shootings at night, or these explosions?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: No. We couldn't. The situation worsened from one day to the next.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And was Serb property damaged as well, or was it just non-Serb property that was damaged?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: No. No Serb property was damaged; only non-Serb property.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just before I move on, how frequent were these explosions of non-Serb property?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: At first not so frequently, but afterwards almost every night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, if you can tell me who was Branko Basara?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Branko Basara was the commander of the 6th Krajina Brigade who came to Sanski Most with his unit from Jasenovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When did you first meet him personally, approximately?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Biscevic, it's -- I think -- I'm seeing you referring to some notes that you have in front of you. I think it's only fair to advise you beforehand that if you will in the course of your testimony make reference or consult some notes, you may be asked to hand them over so that they can be checked; in other words, the Defence, the Tribunal, and everyone has a right to see those notes, copies of those notes, yeah. We'll make copies. So it's your option. You have every right to refer to notes that you may have kept or brought with you to refresh your memory, but if you do you will have to make them available if you are so requested.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a dentist by occupation. I have 40 years of service. I have about a million patients behind me in my career. What happened ten years ago, if you want me to tell you the date I will not be able to do so probably. I just took note of those dates. It's up to you. This happened sometime in March. Mr. Basara with the 6th Krajina Brigade arrived in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't misunderstand me. We -- you are not being criticised at all for referring to notes. One would expect you to have something to help refresh your memory. However, you ought to know that if you have notes which you are going to make use of in order to refresh your memory, you may be required to make them available to us so that we check. It's not a question that you don't have a right to consult those notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And Mr. Biscevic, I'd ask you to try not to refer to those notes, just use your memory. It's okay to tell me if you don't remember something. That's fine. It was ten years ago. And if you need to refresh your memory, we can do that if it's necessary. Now, I have to remember where I was. So sometime in March you met Basara, who you said was commander of the 6th Krajina Brigade. What capacity did you meet him in? How did you meet him? And I don't need the specific date or anything like that, if you remember how it was that you first -- you came to meet him.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: There were incidents on a daily basis, and we requested that the problems be resolved so that we had these daily meetings. And one day when we had a meeting in the municipality, Mr. Basara came and so did Mr. Zeljaja. I think he was a captain or maybe a major from Prijedor, to attend these meetings of ours as representatives of the military of the Yugoslav People's Army. We were glad to see them. He introduced himself and said that he had come with his 6th Corps, that he had brought his army, as he said, to rest after waging war in Croatia, and that they were on leave and they would be on leave for a couple of day, and that there would be no problems. As we were negotiating, the Serbs, Croats and Muslims could not come to an agreement. Then Mr. Basara, as a military figure of authority, said, "You politicians negotiate as you will, but remember there must not be any war. We are guarantors of peace. And if anything should happen, we will take control of it." And that is how I met Mr. Basara. That was my first contact with him. Afterwards I had more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And we'll talk about those further -- further contacts later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, we have approximately three more minutes. So whenever it's convenient for you to stop, if you are switching on to something new, you just tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We could stop now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So we'll have a short break of 15 minutes, resuming immediately after, and then we'll carry on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, Mr. Ackerman, and Mr. Zecevic, it's being suggested that on Thursday - this Thursday - we work in the morning instead of in the afternoon. Would that be acceptable to you? Do you have any other commitments that --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yeah. That's actually problematic for me, Your Honour. But I can see what I can do about reorganising my other commitment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we will postpone -- would you let Madam Chuqing know?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As soon as possible, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is that because we don't have a courtroom available?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. I mean, not something -- if it depended on me, I would opt for it every day, but it doesn't depend on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I will see what I can do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Cayley. So Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you hear me, Mr. Biscevic?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to turn your -- staying in the same time period, if you could tell me a little bit about how weapons were taken from the non-Serb population in Sanski Most. Could you start off by talking -- telling me about the weapons which were held by the TOs or Territorial Defence. If you could tell me where those munitions were normally stored and then if they were moved during 1992.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: I shall try to explain things, to make things clearer for you. First of all, we prohibited Muslims and Croats to report as reservists. Though the order came from the army that they have to respond, otherwise they could go to prison. As we did not accept this, our people did not respond. After that, it was said that non-Serbs need not respond on condition that they handed over their uniforms and their weapons. At the same time we had regular meetings and at one meeting Mr. Nedeljko Rasula, as the town mayor, brought with him a telegram which as he said - and we didn't verify it - had come from Belgrade, according to which the weapons of the Territorial Defence had to be stored in the MUP of Sanski Most. And in addition to the weapons, that the active-duty military had, there were also weapons for the Territorial Defence in companies, enterprises, and other organisations, and there was a room where these weapons were kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, was that order carried out?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely so. A hundred per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did that cause you and the non-Serb population any concern?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: A great deal of concern, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Briefly why was that?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence guaranteed arming in enterprises and local communities and the villages may be mono-ethnic, be it Serb, Croat, or Muslim. And in the municipalities inhabited by Muslims and Croats, if they're left with no weapons, then they have nothing and that is what caused us problems and that is why we were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, at some point were there also orders for civilians to turn over their weapons, their licensed weapons?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: As the weapons of the Territorial Defence were stored in the MUP premises and attached to the MUP, was the building of the military department of the Territorial Defence, then there were daily orders broadcast on the radio station that weapons that had not been handed in, had to be surrendered and no sanctions would be taken, no one would be punished. Licensed weapons and weapons held by the military would not have to be surrendered but only non-registered weapons. That is how it was at first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You say at first. If you can continue. What happened with the licensed weapons?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: After that, again on Radio Sana there was an announcement which said such and such a village or such and such a local community on such and such a day at such and such a time had to bring their weapons and a military truck would arrive with military officers to take over the weapons, the weapons would be taken over, no receipts were given, the weapons were driven away. We didn't know where they went.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You said you -- these announcements would be made over the radio.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: We were told they would be used for the Territorial Defence. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Was radio transmission -- was that the normal way that these announcements would be made, or were they made in other ways?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: No. This was the normal method in those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you or your family personally turn over any weapons as a result of one of these announcements?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was said that at 5.00 in the afternoon a truck would come close to the house for licensed weapons, as both I and my son were hunters we had licensed rifles, carbines, and pistols and we did not -- we surrendered them all and we never received any receipts for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, do you remember what day that was approximately?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: That was just before the attack on Sanski Most, around April or May. It started in April but then it escalated in May, because we have 26 villages so everything was not collected in one day. It took some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And briefly back in -- back to April and the takeover of the municipality building which occurred. You were -- if you understand what I'm referring to, you were in -- you were one of the people in the municipality building before the non-Serbs were ordered to leave; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Before the municipality was taken over, Nedeljko Rasula as the town mayor organised a campaign to take control of the military department and the MUP, then known as the SUP. On that day when the military department and the SUP were taken over, all non-Serb preliminary were simply driven out and from then on Sanski Most only had Serb police. After that they were already able to do more or less what they wanted because they had all the power, the weapons had been seized, so that we were powerless. As they had captured the MUP and the military department, then we said as the municipality building is at the other end of town, then we said we would keep the municipality building, where we would have our own centre; that is, the Croats and the Muslims. And that is when differences arose between us, because this did not suit the Serbs. They had already captured the radio station and the bank, and they didn't want the municipality to be under our control. They -- until then we had meetings amongst ourselves and there were some sorts of agreement amongst ourselves. But it wasn't really agreements. They were giving orders -- so that finally on the 27th of April, as we had been in the municipality for two days already, while we were in the municipality there were talks between us and them. There was a delegation of theirs who came to discuss what they could have in the building. But later on we saw that was a farce. On the 27th of April, at 10.30 they launched a hand grenade. There's a large square and a park next to the municipality. Then there's the post office and the hotel across the way. They positioned two machine-guns, hedge cogs all around so that there was no access. And the military came in front of the municipality building. They were drinking and shooting and acting in an unruly manner: And then they ordered us to abandon the building or they would destroy it. And then a hand grenade was thrown into the cellar. The building was not destroyed, but it was enough for the Croats and the Muslims to climb out of a window and go to the village of Sehovci. On the way there were no problems, though we did see patrols. We saw them standing there, but they didn't cause us any problems and they let us go to this village of Sehovci normally. We stayed there until the next day in the morning. Nothing more happened. Then the municipality was taken over. There was some shooting. And we saw that the shooting was not limited to the area in front of the municipality only but the main road from Prijedor to Kljuc, 1 and a half kilometres away there were machine-gun nests opening fire, and we realised afterwards that this was just a test to check whether the Muslims and the Croats had any weapons and would resist, because they probably thought that we would resist. And as no resistance was put up, we went to this Muslim village, spent the night there. The next day everything was peaceful. We went back and then the next day Mr. Talic intervened and he came by helicopter to Sanski Most and he said that this should not have happened, that Rasula was working on his own, that everything has to be peaceful so that we could continue living peacefully. From that moment on, there were no contacts or meetings between Serbs and non-Serbs. There were no meetings. There were just orders. So whatever they ordered, we had to carry out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The interpreters are asking me to ask you in turn to slow down when you are giving your evidence, because you are giving them too much work. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I get a bit carried away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just to clarify. You were in the municipality building at that time and were one of the people who was forced out of it; correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: The Croats and the Muslims and policemen who were of non-Serb nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But my -- what I just want to clarify is you were actually present at that time and were one of those people; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: On that day I -- I was there. That evening I wasn't in the municipality building, not when the shelling took place, because it was Sunday, it was the weekend, and in the afternoon I went away for the weekend, because I had a farm about 15 kilometres away. At the time there were checkpoints. It was sealed off, and it was impossible to enter anyway. So that evening I wasn't in the building. I wasn't in the building when the hand -- when the grenade was launched.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's important to keep clear what you personally observed and what you've heard about. And similarly you spoke about a meeting where General Talic spoke. You were not at that meeting, were you, the one you've just talked about?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't there. Mr. Mirzet Karabeg was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, after this event with the municipal -- municipality building and the meeting which followed, in the next month you said that you, meaning, I take it, non-Serbs had to do everything they said. Did things calm down? Did they get worse? If you can just briefly tell me, generally, whether things got better after that meeting or whether there continued to be incidents of explosions and shootings and problems.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: On a daily basis -- well, it carried on. It continued in a negative sense. They had military power. This time they had the policemen and they had political power, so that there was no need for them to explain anything to us or to ask us for anything. The 6th Corps of Lieutenant Colonel Basara was there. The reserve forces of the army was there on a daily basis. They were all armed, because from that point in time the reserve forces, the active police, and the active army, they had the legal right to bear weapons. They set up checkpoints at all the crossroads and these checkpoints were manned by armed soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. If I could move up now to the 25th of May, 1992. I want to start talking to you about your personal story, what happened to you and your family after that date. Okay?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: On the 25th of May, the arrests had already started, the arrests of us political leaders, so that Mr. Adil Draganovic had already been arrested as well as Mr. Ico, a Croat whose name I don't know, and four other -- five other men. Mr. Suad Sabic had been taken to MUP -- the MUP for questioning. He was questioned there for a few hours and then a colleague of his -- because the army was down below and he wasn't able to go out, so a colleague of his took him home -- drove him home, and he was arrested the following day. At that time, that was on the 25th, in the evening of the 25th, as I had a goldsmith's shop in the centre of the town. On the 25th, in the evening, next to my shop - because there are about ten other shops there - a Zolja, a grenade was launched at one of the shops in the evening. It was destroyed and the glass was broken, the windows of all the other shops shattered because of the explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And was your shop damaged? I'm sorry. It wasn't clear to me from your answer.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: I can hear the interpreter. I'm waiting for the interpretation to finish. That's why I slowed down a bit. I didn't finish what I had to say. That morning I went there. All the windows -- everything was covered in glass, my shop too. On that day, since it wasn't possible to work, it was panic, I took some boards and boarded up the -- the window. But at 4.00 in the afternoon I was told that the army was stealing from the goldsmith's shop. They'd -- I didn't go there but a relative of mine went there. But that was of no use at all. That evening, on the 26th, an attack was carried out against Sana. That evening there was shooting from all kinds of weapons, and this took place in the town. I was in my house with my family at the time and probably other people too, because we weren't soldiers. We thought that there was just shooting going on in the town. But later on I found out that this had been organised, this shooting had been organised and that the surrounding hills had been taken by the army and the army was firing from above. They were shelling from above, which were aimed at Sanski Most -- which would fall on Sanski Most. When the attack took place -- before that, they said -- they would always say that armed forces have been surrendered but not a sufficient number of arms. They would say, "Since Mahala has just Muslim population, 10 per cent of the people there haven't surrendered the weapons. They should do so or the entire village shall be destroyed."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me ask you. When you were walking through the town of Sanski Most on the 26th of May, did you see any Muslims or Croats armed walking around or did you see any armed resistance by Muslims or Croat civilians or any non-Serbs at that time on that day?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Not a single one. We were only able to take sticks and go to war, because there was nothing else to take.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let's move ahead one day to the 27th of May, 1992. What happened to you at around 1.00 p.m. That day?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: At 1.00 in the afternoon, three vehicles arrived, the army arrived. They called me out. They said I had to go to a meeting urgently to some sort of talks, that I was being summoned. A white Mercedes and two other vehicles arrived. I was put in the Mercedes, in the middle. There were two soldiers at the back and two at the front. When I got in, they said that they had been ordered to handcuff me and take me in. They handcuffed me as I was sitting in the middle and they were sitting at the sides and there probably wasn't enough room so they put the handcuffs at the front. My hands were in front of me. They took me to the MUP building. I was left in the corridor there facing the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you for a minute. You were arrested at your home at 1.00 p.m. Where was your wife and your three sons at that point when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: The attack against Sanski Most was in the evening, and then over the Radio Sana they said, "We're now stopping with the attack for two hours because in Gornja Mahala where the Muslims were in the majority all the weapons hadn't surrendered and they would surrender the weapons in two hours time all will be destroyed." My son, the eldest son, Haris, that evening, as he had a girlfriend, she was in our house and she spent the night there. During those two hours when there was no shooting, as her father had had called her, he went to take her to her home. My wife and myself and my two youngest son, who were twins, we were in our house, we remained in our family house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry I interrupted you. Before I interrupted you, you were saying you were taken to the MUP after you were arrested at 1.00 p.m. Can you tell me what happened when you arrived there.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: I waited for some time in the MUP. The policemen who went there with me, they went off somewhere, and they came back very quickly. They ordered me to get into the car again and I passed through the town then I saw that everything was burning in the town, the Muslim part, where the shops were, that part was all burning. It had been destroyed. They drove me through the town. And as I know the town of Sanski Most, they took me to a village on the outskirts of Sanski Most. This village was called Magarice. When we got there - that's about 3 or 4 kilometres from the MUP - when they took me up there, that's a peasant place where Serbs live. There was a house and a barn, a place where meat would be smoked. And then I saw -- up until then I didn't know this, but I saw that there were a lot of soldiers and there and lot of weapons, because you go along the side. And as I was going along the side, there's a forest and then there are fields and then I saw that they had boxes of weapons, about 60 by 80 centimetres and 50 centimetres high. They were piled up for about 2 metres and about 15 metres they extended to a length of about 15 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And which soldiers were --

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: And below at each -- every 10 metres -- as I'm a dentist, I don't understand these things. But later on I heard that these were mortars. These are small mortars. On a tripod there's one barrel and then they'd put the shells in them and they would fire. Every 10 metres they had positioned these mortars and they had binoculars. That's what you use when you're put -- when you're determining the area, the geographical area, and they could see everything with that. And then later, as I had been imprisoned - I spent about 30 hours imprisonment - I saw that they were observing through these devices and trying to decide which buildings to destroy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me slow you down a little bit. You were taken up to this village Magarice and you said you saw a lot of soldiers. Do you know -- well, I'll move on. Which -- what happened when you got there? Were you taken out of the car?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: When we got there, they took me out of the car. Then they -- we went straight ahead, because there was an orchard there. We went -- right in front of us. I knew Basara personally. I saw that he was sitting there and an officer was with him. There was a table there in the garden and there was a map of Sanski Most there. There was a litre of brandy. They were sitting and drinking and looking at the map. And then I saw there was a communication with Radio Sanski Most, because I could see wires which probably went as far as Sana radio station. When I got there, I approached them and I said, "Good day." The second person didn't say anything. Basara pretended not to know me and said nothing. The other one cursed me. He cursed my balija God and he said, "Come with me." He then took me behind the orchard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you. You said that you -- Basara was there. How do you know that was Basara? You said he -- he acted as though he didn't know. How are you sure that that was Branko Basara that you met on the day you're telling us about?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: We were in contact. We had attended quite a few meetings together. We had discussed -- drank coffee together. So I knew him. He probably felt uneasy, so -- so he bowed his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And then what happened after you said this person who was with him, this officer, began to curse -- curse at you and verbally abuse you?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: He took me out of those grounds. He took me to the meadows which were above the town. And it was a nice sunny day, so you could see the town. You could see everything. Everything was very clear. And then he cursed me and he said, "Look. You can see what you did to us." The town was burning -- the entire town was burning, both the Muslim and the Croatian part of the town was burning, because that's a special part of town where the neighbourhoods join each other, so everything was burning. He then took me back. I thought he was going to kill me, but he took me back. He sat me down at a table. He gave me a sheet of paper, and he said, "Write." He gave me a sheet of paper, and he said, "Write." What was I to write? So when he came and saw that there was nothing -- but before that, before that, when he was taking me back, two soldiers were waiting. There was an orchard where there were plum trees and a little sort of valley. Two soldiers were waiting. He didn't ask them anything and he didn't say anything to them. They just took me over. But I forgot to say when he saw that my handcuffs were -- my hands were in front of me and I had handcuffs, he cursed them and said, "How are you escorting him?"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Who's he? Who said that?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: This major. Not Basara but this officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: "Put those handcuffs behind his back and make sure that they're as tight as possible." And as I have larger bones, this hurt me. I am a big man. This had to be behind my back. It was very difficult for me. When we were turning, when he showed me the town, then two soldiers simply took me -- took me from him. They took me to that orchard then. They first took my documents, my papers, since I have all of them here. Then they searched me, took everything out of my pockets, my money, my driving licence, and then they started beating me. I don't know for how long they beat me, but it was probably a long time. All I know is that I broke the handcuffs. When they saw that the handcuffs were broken, when I was no longer able to resist, then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Take your time. It's all right. We can take a break whenever you want.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: It's not necessary. It's not necessary to take a break. They took some rope and they tied my hands in front of me. And then he said, "Write." I didn't know what to write. After is certain period of time had passed, he took a Skorpion, hit me in the ears -- above the ears and he said, "What I'm going to say you have to read." The soldiers put me in the car again, took me to the town. I didn't know where. They took me to the radio station.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you before we get to the radio station. When you were beaten in the orchard by these soldiers and you say that the handcuffs broke, what were they -- how were they beating you? With their hands or with sticks or -- I know it's difficult, but if you just describe it a little bit.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: They had their official truncheons and sticks, and they would beat us with both. And they would hit us in the head, the kidneys, the legs, in front. They would hit us in the kidneys.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then you said that -- and I'm not sure if the translation -- I think it came out as that you were hit in the ear with a pistol. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: That was Basara. He didn't hit me. But he shot concern he fired a shot from a Skorpion and said, "This is what is waiting for you and your family if you don't read." I didn't know what he was talking about, what he meant if I didn't read.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when you were -- you said up here you were told to write. Were you told what to write? Were you told what words to put on this piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: He said, "Write," and he left me there for a few minutes. When he returned, there was nothing there. I simply didn't know what to write about. I didn't know about what it was necessary to write, what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And just before we move on, you said that you could look down at the town and see buildings burning. We're talking about the town of Sanski Most. What was the attitude of the soldiers there while this was going on, if you observed that?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: They were quite relaxed. They felt sure of themselves. They sang. They drank. You could hear shooting. You know, for fun. They weren't shooting at the city. So they -- I knew some of the reservists and some people from Sanski Most. They simply pretended that they didn't know me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, let's move on. You were telling us about how after this beating and these events, you were taken by car to the radio station. And can you just tell me approximately -- where is that radio station located in general?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: About 4 kilometres perhaps from that part. We drove there. They took me to the radio station. And when I entered I found a sheet of paper. There was some text on it. They made me sit down. There were two soldiers at my sides. They were pointing Kalashnikovs at my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, who brought you to the radio station? Civilians, police, or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: No, soldiers. Camouflage uniforms. They weren't policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When you got to the --

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: They weren't civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When you got to the radio station, was there anybody that you knew there? Did you know any of the people who worked had? Who was there besides these two soldiers you said were pointing guns at you?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: When I got there, opposite me -- the speaker of Sanski Most radio station was sitting. Later I heard he was the director of the main Sana Radio. Because before that that was Muslim who was expelled and imprisoned and taken to a camp when I got there. Since I knew him -- his mother knew me. She was a teacher of mine. His father was the chief of the station. So he was a well-known person. He was younger than me. I wasn't in contact with him, but I knew who this person was. He simply shrugged his shoulders as if to say there was nothing he could do. That things were as they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: First of all he read something out. "We've captured the most terrible extremist." That's what I heard. I didn't listen to that tape. "We've found a soldier of Alija, representative of the party. It's his fault for everything. He's one of the most extreme persons." And then I was ordered to read that text.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that text was something that had been placed -- that you'd never seen before that day.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: No. No. And -- Badnjevic Ferid, one of the first ones that was there, his nickname was Fajdo. I didn't even know Ferid. He had a cafe in the village where Basara went every day. Later I found out that it was Fajdo who was in question and I was surprised that he had been mentioned as one of the main extremists. He was a friend of Basara's, but that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. At this point I'd like to play a tape recording to the Chamber, have the witness identify it. I hope everybody has a transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's check on that first. Correct me if I am wrong, Mr. Nicholls, transcript in the original B/C/S is 01104873, the first page? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have to -- Ms. Gustin says yes, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And the English version is ERN number 01907754 being the first page?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I have confirmation from the interpreters that they have a copy of each?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Defence? All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The tape is in B/C/S. It will be translated as it's played. And I believe on the English version the first page should be page 5 of the English translation of what we'll hear. It should be keyed up to start at the section which is headed "Female voice," which is just before we get to the main statement

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] We call upon the inhabitants of Podbrijezje to bring all their weapons and military equipment to the crossroads at the checkpoint by 1800 hours. If not, at exactly 1810 hours we will begin to shell the village. If the order is not complied with, we will not bear moral or material responsibility for the consequences of the shelling. The Serbian armed forces have captured the greatest Muslim and Croatian extremist in the Sanski Most municipality Faik Biscevic who attempted to flee from the town. This extremist will address the Croatian and Muslim people over the radio and explain the reasons why he involved them in the war. Announcement, that all Muslims and Croats unconditionally hand over all the weapons they possess legally and illegally and that they surrender to the Serbian army and government because this is a Serbian town. To avoid the soldiers having to use force to locate and seize weapons, it would be better to hand over the weapons voluntarily otherwise Sana will continue to be destroyed until final capitulation. That is why we call upon all the citizens of Sana, Muslims and Croats, to hand over their weapons straight away which would be better for them than to have the town continue to be destroyed. That is why I ask you to see reason and without delay, hand over all the weapons and surrender to the legitimate Serbian authorities. This has to be done immediately. The weapons have to be handed over in order for the destruction of the town for which I bear most of the blame to cease. That is why again I call on all Muslims and Croats to immediately hand over their weapons and recognise the legitimate Serbian authorities so that the legitimate authorities can start functioning as soon as possible and the destruction of the town can end. The Serbian armed forces guarantee the safety of all loyal Muslim and Croatian citizens and I recommend to all Alijas and Tudjman's extremists -- and I am their greatest follower in Sanski Most -- not to lead their people into further bloodshed. I, Redzo Kurbegovic, Mirzet Karabeg, Suad Sabic, Hasib Kamber, Ferid Burnic, Enver Burnic, Nihad Kljucanin, Ekrem Medic, Nedzad Muhic, Eniz Sabanovic, Ahmed Paunovic, Hase Osmancevic, Fahrudin Prsic, Arif Hodzic, Hidajet Dudic, Arif Muhanovic, Fikret Agic, Muhamed Smajlovic, Muhamed Arapovic, Mehmed Alagic, Ibro Pasic, Omer Krupic, Enisa Kurbegovic, Ibro Krickovic, Vahid Fajdo Badnjevic, Safet Avdic, Vahid Handanagic, Suad Cehic, Ismet Ico Avdic and his two brothers, Tale Zahirovic, Murahem Handanagic, Taib Crnkic, Hamza Rekic, Fuad Kurbegovic, Osman Talic, Dervis Hamzic, Elhad Talic, and Basic - I don't know his first name but he works in Borac Travnik in Lusci Palanka - are guilty for everything that has happened recently. That is why we are prepared, on the orders of the Serb armed forces to come out before our people and to be judged by our people in the next few days. I assure you that the command of the Serbian armed forces which is carrying out the armed activities in Sanski Most was forced into such behaviour by our lies and sycophancy. I call on all my sympathisers to join me to surrender to the Serbian armed forces since that is the way we can stop the further bloodshed of our people. Sehovci, Poljak, Sasina, Podbrijezje and Caplje are to collect --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you recognise the voice on the tape we just heard, the long passage?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Whose voice is it?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's give it a number, please, now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the tape and the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be P827.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What, the tape or --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The tape. Let's make that the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Then that would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: A and B?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's fine, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Is that okay with you as well? P827. Follow the usual sequence, Madam Registrar, with A and B representing the English and the B/C/S versions. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That was your voice -- that's a statement you were -- that you read at gunpoint that day in the radio station in Sanski Most; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Two Kalashnikovs. Two soldiers, one on each side with two Kalashnikovs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that's the same statement that we've just heard that you were forced to read that same day? The same words, the same statement? That's a correct recording is what I'm trying to establish with you.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, that was your voice but --

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That statement, was it in any way voluntary on your part, making that statement over the radio?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: My question is: Did you voluntarily make that statement?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: I think that's a superfluous question. I had two Kalashnikovs on each side of my head, and I didn't even know whether my family members had been arrested or not. They had already been arrested, in fact, by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand. And it is a silly question, but there will probably be a couple more slightly silly questions that I have to ask you when I'm trying to establish something for the record. Now, all of those names which you read off as -- in that statement - and I won't repeat them all - as being extremists who were in league with you. Did you know who all these people were, those names you were reading?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Some of them I didn't. I did know most of them, but some I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, those people whose names you did know, were those dangerous people? Were those people of danger to anybody in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: No. They were respected citizens, doctors, lawyers, judges, businessmen, and they were all in the camp with me, each and every one of them. If he wasn't killed, then he was with me in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We'll get to that. Now, after you -- let me ask you this: After you made that statement on the radio - you were forced to make it - did you hear that statement personally later? Do you know if that statement was replayed or not?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: After spending 30 hours in the room used for smoking meat, they took me to the prison in Sanski Most. In the prison in Sanski Most -- when we were going to eat, we left the cells. And also in the cell, as the radio was tuned in loud upstairs where the Territorial Defence was, so that for five or six days I kept listening to myself speaking, though in fact I was in the cell. So I did hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, after you leave the radio station I think you just said you're taken back to Magarice. Is that where -- were you taken back to the same place, the same area where you had been given that severe beating you were telling us about earlier?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: They took me there. And when they took me back, the major was no longer there but only Lieutenant Colonel Basara was there. They continued beating. So they dragged me more or less. And he said, "Take that man down there." And then they said to me, "Major" - whether it was Brajic or Vukovic, I'm not sure of the surname - "explicitly ordered that he must be here." So they shut me up in that curing room, hut, where I spent 30 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And was there anybody else in that hut with you during that -- during that 30-hour period? Were you alone?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: When I got there, I was alone. I was the first to be thrown in there. However, the next day, when it dawned, Hamza Rekic was brought in and then Asim, a male nurse. I don't remember his name. They behaved in the same way. When they brought them in, these two soldiers would first loot them, beat them up, and then bring them to where I was. They told Hamza Rekic to come, and he came with his own Mercedes, and then they shut him up. As for Asim, he was a young man. He was collecting the hay. They found him there, and they brought him to Magarice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And while you were in there -- you've described it as a hut. I take it as some small wooden shack or small wooden structure. Correct me if that's wrong. Could you hear anything going on outside while you were in there for those 30 hours or so?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Everything could be heard loud and clear. First of all, they had gathered in large numbers. They had heard on Radio Sana - because there were loudspeakers everywhere - that I had been arrested. And as they knew me. They said, "We've caught Alija's combatant." This curing shack is about 2 metres by 2, and they're simple boards, and there's a space between them, and then some of them would come and try and stab me with the bayonets. When I got there, I saw what it was. Kemal Malovcic is a singer, a well-known singer, and he had a very nice villa in a Muslim settlement, and they kept saying "Kemal's villa." And they would say, "We've missed it," and then suddenly they would all scream out, "We've hit it, and it's burning." So they were simply targeting these buildings and destroying them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just another silly question. When you say "they" and "them" all through the statement you just made, you're talking about Serb soldiers -- 6th Krajina soldiers -- 6th Krajina Corps soldiers?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Again, they -- the army, the Yugoslav People's Army, had a truck. In front there were boards. And you could just see the barrel of a machine-gun peeping out. When I got to Magarice, I got trucks -- I saw a canteen, I saw an APC, and I saw a very large number of troops. They would come to sleep there. They didn't sleep in town, they slept there, so that I knew that that was where they were -- that their headquarters were. Basara was there and another major and the command and a radio station they used to issue orders about all operations that were going on down in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And you said that you were held there in this shack for 30 hours. Where were you -- what happened after that 30 hours? Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: At 12.00 at night they took us out where the canteen was and they gave us some macaroni, some pasta. Each one of us got a plateful of macaroni to eat because we hadn't eaten anything for 30 hours. When we had eaten it, there were three cars that were brought there and they put one of us in each car. There was -- I was in the middle, two soldiers on each side, a third next to the driver, and the driver. And all three had Kalashnikovs pointed at my head. As it was midnight and as all three car were going, I thought that we were going to be executed. Where else would they take us at that time of night? But that didn't happen. They took us to the prison in the town of Sanski Most itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm not sure when exactly we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have approximately one minute more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think we may as well break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's a good time to break, actually, because there's a new chapter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we need to stop here, because that's the time we have allocated to us. We will continue tomorrow. Do you think you will be in a position to finish your examination-in-chief tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it depends, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, obviously. But more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We are going to conduct the cross-examination anyhow, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, try and conclude it tomorrow then. Yes. You will be escorted out of this courtroom by the usher, and you will return here tomorrow at 2.15. Hopefully there won't be the same delay as there was today, because you will be the first witness and we will start straight away according to our schedule. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, tomorrow we will be sitting in this same courtroom, Courtroom I. I don't know about Thursday which courtroom would that be if we work in the morning, which courtroom would that be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Still Courtroom I perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Still courtroom --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: But I will confirm for you tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But we will wait, of course, confirmation from Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, to be frank with you, you should go ahead anyway. What concerns me at the moment as you know Ms. Korner is in another trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I know that you have a desire that at least one of us be present in the courtroom. Tomorrow I do have a problem. I've got an engagement that is actually linked to Thursday, so I will not be here. And it's unlikely that Ms. Korner will not be here either. But what we will try to do is get another lawyer to sit in. It's unfortunately unavoidable and it's not something we anticipated was going to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's take it -- be more practical about it. This witness, I suppose will finish tomorrow. I hope so at least. Lets anticipate that we will finish with him tomorrow. Then the next one will be 7.139; who will be examining?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Ms. Richterova, and that is who I'm hoping will be able to sit in and replace me tomorrow with Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That should be enough. I think we could move -- move ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if you do have a problem, do let me know. And if there is a problem with the Defence, any prior commitments or anything, do let me know as well. Okay? So we'll meet again tomorrow. We'll resume tomorrow at 2.15. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: at 6.32 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 19th day of June, 2002, at 2.15 p.m. 25
